newsitem.title: MEXICO: Peso falls to lowest level of year, stocks tumble.
newsitem.headline: Peso falls to lowest level of year, stocks tumble.

text.p: The peso fell to its lowest level this year and stock prices tumbled Monday as investors gave a thumbs down to news the government was scaling back plans to sell off parts of the state-run petrochemicals business.
The benchmark 48-hour peso closed a hefty six centavos weaker at 7.73/7.74 to the dollar -- it's weakest closing level since last December.
The weaker peso fuelled expectations that local interest rates would rise sharply on Tuesday to stem a speculative run on the currency, and that knocked down stock prices on the Mexican stock market.
The leading IPC index fell 47.77 points, or 1.4 percent, to 3,287.38 on weak volume of 47 million shares. There were 74 losers and just 11 gainers.
Traders expected the peso to come under renewed selling pressure on Tuesday as U.S. markets reopened.
"(An adjustment of the peso) was more or less expected ... what worries me is the speed at which the peso is adjusting," said a peso trader.

Economists said the peso was due for a correction after big gains against the dollar this year caused some to question whether it was again becoming overvalued -- as it was before the spectacular December 1994 peso crash that rocked the Mexican economy and sent shudders through world financial markets.
Some exporters added recently to the growing chorus of concern about the peso by pointing to a declining trade surplus as a consequence of a stronger peso.
"The feeling was the peso was too strong, so people latched on to any excuse to sell," said Damian Fraser, director of analysis at Caspian Research in Mexico City.

The excuse may have been the government's announcement on Sunday that it had called off its four-year-old project to sell 100 percent of its secondary petrochemical plants -- offering joint government-private sector ventures instead.

Although Mexico has already sold off most of its previously state-owned industries, some investors fear it will never get around to selling the oil and gas sectors still in government hands. Privatisation of the country's railroads has also been badly delayed.
The peso recovered after panic selling in the morning led it to a midday low of 7.780/7.7850 per dollar.
Stocks market dealers said they were worried that peso weakness could force interest rates to reverse their recent drop and begin moving sharply higher.
On Monday, market heavyweight Telmex L shares fell 12 centavos (two cents) to 12.24 pesos ($1.58).
